To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the three-flavor quasiparticle model of quark matter is a viable alternative to color-superconducting quark matter in neutron stars and (2) the sequential deconfinement scenario is a viable alternative in the sense that it leads to stable hybrid stars and is compatible with the existence of quark-matter cores in neutron stars.

1) A two-flavor color-superconducting phase of dense matter is realized in the cores of neutron stars, 2) The transition from hadronic to quark matter occurs at a density of about 3 times nuclear saturation density and 3) The quark matter phase in the core of neutron stars is a two-flavor, type II color superconductor.

(1) the quark-matter phase in the center of massive neutron stars may be a two-flavor superconductor (2SC) or a color-flavor locked (CFL) phase and (2) the transition from nuclear matter to quark matter occurs at high densities, n{sub QM} {approx} 3n{0}, which is consistent with the results of other groups.

the development of new methods for the treatment of the quantum-mechanical many-body problem in the presence of strong interactions.
the study of the properties of neutron stars, in particular the equation of state (EOS) and its consequences for the maximum mass of neutron stars.
the study of the properties of neutron stars, which are believed to be formed in supernova explosions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a model for the quark phase of neutron stars, based on the Nambu-Jon-Lasinio (N.J.L) model.

we have shown that the three light quarks in cold asymmetric nuclear systems are sequentially deconfimed at densities above the nuclear saturation density n{sub 1}. In particular, we have shown that nucleons are dissociated via d-quark dripping at about n{sub 2} = 2 n{sub 3} and that a two-flavor quark matter phase with color superconductivity is realized at n{sub 4} = 2n{sub 2}.
we have studied the properties of quark matter and nuclear matter in the context of neutron star physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a neutron star can be composed of three different phases, namely nuclear matter, quark matter and mixed phase, and the quark matter can be in two different phases.
the deconfined phase in the core of neutron stars can be a two-flavor (2SC) rather than a three-flavor (CFL) color superconducting phase.
a quark matter phase with a nonvanishing diquark gap can be formed at moderate baryon densities.
